title: The Language of Specialists
text:
Every specialised field develops a vocabulary that outsiders find opaque. Radiologists speak of a 'ground-glass opacity' to describe a hazy patch on a lung scan, while structural engineers invoke 'hysteresis' to describe a material that retains a memory of previous stress. Such jargon is not merely ornamental; it compresses long descriptions into single terms that practitioners can use with precision. Consequently, mastery of a discipline's lexicon is often as revealing of expertise as any formal qualification.

Yet jargon carries a hidden cost. When specialists address a general audience without translating their terms, they can inadvertently exclude the very people they need to persuade, such as patients deciding on treatment or citizens voting on infrastructure. Skilled communicators therefore alternate between technical and plain language, deploying the former for colleagues and the latter for everyone else. The ability to switch registers gracefully is, in this sense, a more demanding skill than the mere command of terminology.

questions.text: According to the second paragraph, which group might be excluded when specialists use jargon without translating it?
What can be inferred about the authors' view of expertise?
options: Command of a field's vocabulary is considered a meaningful sign of expertise
Expertise is measured only by formal qualifications
Jargon should be abandoned entirely by experts
Engineers are better communicators than radiologists

questions.text: Which claim best follows from the passage's final sentence about switching registers?
options: Adapting one's language to the audience is a harder skill than knowing technical terms
Plain language is always preferred over technical language
Technical terms should be memorised only by beginners
Switching registers requires no special training

paragraph_translations: Cada campo especializado desarrolla un vocabulario que resulta opaco para los ajenos a él. Los radiólogos hablan de una 'ground-glass opacity' para describir una mancha turbia en un escáner de pulmón, mientras que los ingenieros estructurales invocan la 'histéresis' para describir un material que conserva la memoria de tensiones previas. Esta jerga no es meramente ornamental; condensa descripciones largas en términos únicos que los profesionales pueden usar con precisión. En consecuencia, dominar el léxico de una disciplina revela la experiencia tanto como cualquier título formal.

Sin embargo, la jerga tiene un coste oculto. Cuando los especialistas se dirigen a un público general sin traducir sus términos, pueden excluir sin querer a las mismas personas que necesitan convencer, como los pacientes que deciden un tratamiento o los ciudadanos que votan sobre infraestructuras. Por ello, los comunicadores hábiles alternan entre el lenguaje técnico y el lenguaje llano: el primero para los colegas y el segundo para todos los demás. En este sentido, la capacidad de cambiar de registro con soltura es una habilidad más exigente que el mero dominio de la terminología.
